pages.title: Performance and Shaders
pages.text:
[#](FFFFFF)[#]() **Key points**

- Give the game **8 GB** of RAM on a 16 GB PC, or **12 GB** on a big one. More than 16 GB doesn't help.
- Shaders are optional: Options > Video Settings > Shader Packs.
- If it stutters, turn Distant Horizons down first.
- The first world takes a while to create.

This is a heavy pack. Give the game **8 GB of RAM** on a 16 GB PC, or **12 GB** on a big one, in your launcher's instance settings. More than 16 GB doesn't help. The README has the matching Java flags.

**Distant Horizons** draws far-away terrain as simplified [#](7A3C9A)[chunks](entry://glossary/chunk)[#]() so you can see much further than normal render distance. It is useful for airships and the Moon, but costs memory and some frame rate. Holes near you while flying fast fill in once the chunks arrive.\
\
[#](FFFFFF)[#]() **Tip:** turn its settings down first if the game stutters.

pages.title: Distant Horizons
pages.text: Shows far terrain as simplified chunks. Handy from an airship, a submarine or the Moon.

**On a laptop** (16 GB RAM):

- Give the game 8 GB, no more.
- Play plugged in.
- Set Distant Horizons' render distance to 128 or lower; the pack ships 256.
- Render distance 10, simulation distance 8.
- Skip shaders, or use Solas, the lightest.
- Don't host the server on it while you play.

**Shaders** are included and run through Iris. Open Options > Video Settings > Shader Packs to pick one.

- Complementary Reimagined, with Euphoria Patches
- Bliss
- Photon
- Solas

For Bliss or Photon, pick the copy ending in **+ Clrwl** so contraptions are shaded right.

**DLAA** (optional) works only with the shader pack **Photon v1.3a + DLAA**, a copy of Photon + Clrwl the pack makes at startup: pick it under Shader Packs. It replaces Photon's own anti-aliasing with NVIDIA DLSS or AMD FSR 3.1: a sharper picture with far less shimmer on leaves, fences and water.

Its settings are on the **Upscaling** tab behind the **Upscaling & Display...** button at the top of the shader pack menu (also Mods > Create Galore Bridge > Config). **Auto** uses NVIDIA DLAA on an RTX card and FSR 3.1 on any other card.

DLSS needs your own nvngx\_dlss.dll, which isn't part of the pack. **Find on this PC** copies it from where the NVIDIA app keeps its DLSS downloads. If there's none, use **Get from NVIDIA** and **Open DLSS folder**. The screen shows the version it has.

The DLSS preset is K unless you pick J, L, M or type another letter; a letter DLSS has no preset for runs as K. If DLAA can't run, a notice says why and Photon keeps its own anti-aliasing. If the game closes while DLSS or FSR starts, that one stays off until you press **Try again** on the settings screen. Log lines about it start with DLAA:.

**Render resolution** on that screen trades sharpness for frames. Native draws every pixel. Quality (67%%), Balanced (58%%), Performance (50%%) and Ultra Performance (33%%) draw the scene smaller and DLSS or FSR fill in the window. Custom has a slider from 25%% to 100%%.\
\
With the anti-aliasing Off, Photon's own upscaler does the job, softer.

With an RTX card, Quality looks like Native and runs faster; Performance is a little softer and faster still. FSR looks best at Quality.\
\
From Balanced down, presets L and M are worth a try: L is the sharpest at Performance.

L and M also keep underwater light shafts and the specks in the water clean, where K and FSR smear them a little.\
\
They are made for RTX 40 and 50 cards; on RTX 20 and 30 cards they cost more frames, so stay on K there if the frame rate drops.

**Ray Reconstruction** (experimental, RTX cards) is on the Upscaling tab too. NVIDIA's DLSS Ray Reconstruction takes DLSS's place and also cleans up Photon's lighting: water reflects like glass, shadows stay sharp and still, and torchlight on metal stays crisp.

It costs frames: on an RTX 4080 SUPER, Ray Reconstruction at Performance runs nearly as fast as DLSS at Quality. It needs NVIDIA's nvngx\_dlssd.dll (**Find on this PC** copies it) and an NVIDIA driver 580 or newer.

Turning it on sets Photon to **Ultra** the first time; after that you get the changes you made in Photon's menu while it was on. Turning it off brings back your own Photon settings. A message says so each time.

Photon's menu stays yours to change while Ray Reconstruction runs, but whatever you set, soft shadows and reflections are left grainy for it to clean up, and rough blocks like metal get blurry reflections they don't have with it off. So Photon at High looks different with it than without it.
Ray Reconstruction shows its worth most at Photon's highest settings, with every lighting effect on. At lower settings there is little for it to clean up.

Shaders are optional and can cut frame rate a lot on weaker machines. First world creation is also slow because of how many mods add world generation. This settles after the first load.\
\
Name tags are drawn after the shader, so they stay readable with every pack.\
\
**Fullscreen** is F11. Screenshot key: F2.

**Ambiance** runs only on your own PC: sound echoes in caves, footsteps, falling leaves, held torches that light up, smoother animations. It changes nothing in play. A torch in your hand looks bright but doesn't stop mobs spawning; place one for that. Fresh Animations can be turned off under Resource Packs.

**Chunksmith** pregenerates terrain when you ask it to with the **/cs** commands, ahead of an airship or train. It yields to players, so you can keep playing while it runs. Its automatic run on world entry (a 4096-block radius every time you join) is switched off here.

[#](FFFFFF)[#]() **In depth.** On an NVIDIA card with a 10-bit monitor, set Vulkan/OpenGL present method to Prefer layered on DXGI Swapchain in the NVIDIA Control Panel, or the driver still switches a 10-bit monitor to 8-bit. With shaders this can cap the GPU at about half its speed; set it back to Auto if you don't need 10-bit.

**Black strobing** after that change can happen on some GPUs and drivers. It shows up when VSync (or adaptive VSync) is on and Max Framerate is Unlimited. Fix: turn VSync off (RivaTuner can then cap FPS smoothly), or cap Max Framerate at or below your monitor's refresh rate.

**Perfect Presentation** (Windows) shows the game through DirectX: fullscreen is a fast borderless window, Alt-Tab is instant and a 10-bit monitor stays 10-bit. It is switched on or off in the display settings (the **Upscaling & Display...** button in the shader pack menu, **Display** tab); restart after. On NVIDIA, set Power management mode to Prefer maximum performance for javaw.exe.

**DirectX** (same tab) picks what Perfect Presentation runs on: **12** or **11**. In tests 12 gave marginally lower input delay at the same frame rate, and frame generation needs it. Picking 12 turns Perfect Presentation on; restart once. Where 12 can't start, the game runs on 11 and the screen says so.

**NVIDIA Reflex** (Windows, NVIDIA GTX 900 or newer, experimental) is on the same tab. The driver starts each frame as late as it can, and the game reads the mouse just before it draws, so the view follows the mouse sooner. It works best with a Max Framerate the card can hold. Picking it turns on Perfect Presentation, which it needs: restart once.

**GPU pacing** (any card, same tab) is for playing uncapped. The game waits just before drawing each frame, so the frame doesn't queue on the card and the view follows the mouse sooner. **On** keeps the frame rate; **Lowest** cuts a little more delay for about 6%% fewer frames.\
\
A **Max Framerate** the card can hold gives the shortest delay of all, on any card.

**Frame generation** (same tab) shows a frame of its own between every two the game draws, so motion looks about twice as smooth, for a little more input delay. **DLSS** runs where NVIDIA's own check says the card can (RTX 40 and 50); if not, the setting says why. **FSR** runs on other cards too and is best from about 60 fps. Both need DLSS or FSR anti-aliasing.

Picking one turns on Perfect Presentation and DirectX 12 (DLSS also turns on Reflex): restart once. After that it turns on and off at once; switching between DLSS and FSR needs a restart. DLSS also needs Windows' Hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling and NVIDIA's nvngx\_dlssg.dll: **Find on this PC** on the Upscaling tab copies it.
With frame generation on, **Max Framerate** counts the frames on screen, with DLSS and with FSR: a cap of 120 shows 120 frames a second, 60 drawn by the game and 60 made between them.

On cards where NVIDIA's own check says DLSS can make more than one frame between two (RTX 50), the list also has **DLSS 3x** and **DLSS 4x**: two or three frames of its own for each one the game draws. They work like DLSS (2x), which was tested, but haven't been tried on an RTX 50 card yet, hence the red **\***. At 4x a cap of 120 shows 120 frames, 30 drawn by the game.

Where NVIDIA's check says the card and driver run it, there is also **DLSS Dynamic**, untried on RTX 50 as well. It leaves the game's own frame rate alone and changes how many frames it adds, scene by scene, to fill your monitor's refresh rate.

With 2x, 3x or 4x the multiplier stays put and the game is held to a steady share of the refresh rate, which feels steadier. **Dynamic** keeps input delay lower while the game runs fast, but you may notice it switching.

The **NVIDIA app** can change the model DLSS frame generation uses: Graphics, Global Settings, **DLSS Override - Model Presets**, Frame Generation. It works here, though NVIDIA's overlay reads "FG OVR N/A". On an RTX 4080 SUPER, **Preset C** drew about 6%% more frames with a little less input delay; **Preset B** ran like NVIDIA's own pick.

**Frame counter** on the same tab: **Basic** shows the frame rate in a corner; **Detailed** adds the frame time, the 1%% and 0.1%% lows and a graph of the last few seconds. Pick the **Corner**. **Dim for OLED** keeps it faint and moves it a pixel now and then so it can't burn in. F3 and F1 hide it.
